This article completely misses the reason that the West is concerned about ISIS. It has nothing to do with them being a direct threat, but it has everything to do with them destabilizing a strategically important region.

The Middle East may only provide less than 10% of the US' oil imports, but the US economy is tied to regions such as Asia and Europe, who receive most of their oil and large portions of their overall energy consumption from the Middle East.

ISIS, with its predilection for seizing oil fields as a source of income, represents a threat in this capacity, as well as their ability to attract large amounts of support both within the region and outside the region.

ISIS is growing incredibly fast, and at this point there's no clear strategy for halting their growth and expansion. If ISIS is given a free pass to act as they see fit, then you can bet that they will expand and seize even more of the region's strategic resources, creating a situation where the U.S. or other Western powers will have little if any say on the region's policies, and this could have serious economic ramifications.

Now personally, I believe that we never should have been involved in the politics of the region in the first place, but now that we are involved we cannot easily extricate ourselves. The only thing holding ISIS back are US and Iran supported fighters. If the US pulls out, then you'll end up with all of the Sunni fighters joining ISIS (as is what happened in Syria already), and all the Shiite fighters joining the militias which are essentially puppets of Iran.

We do have an interest in the Middle East, and ISIS is a threat to that interest. The interest is economic though, and you'll never see a politician say that they want to combat ISIS because they want to protect the oil--it's political suicide and would only serve to get ISIS more support.

Is the ISIS threat "overblown?" Only if you think that the threat is what the politicians are saying.
